opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a fairly simple observation: the way most people approach embodied AI today is to take a model trained for something else, like a large language model or a vision-language model trained on internet images and text, and then bolt an action head onto it. That works to a degree, but I always felt it was backwards.

Those models learned about the world by reading and looking. They never had to *act* in it. Their whole representation of the world is built around describing things, not around how things move, how forces propagate, or what happens when you push on an object. So when you ask them to control a robot, you're asking a model that has spent its entire "life" as an observer to suddenly become a participant. You can fine-tune it, but the underlying priors are still the priors of a spectator.

For me, an embodied-native model means that from the very beginning, the core thing the model learns is the relationship between perception, action, and consequence. Physical interaction isn't an add-on capability. It's the foundation. Language and vision are still important, but they should serve the embodied loop, not the other way around.

There's also a practical reason. If you start from a language-centric model, you inherit its architecture, its tokenization, and its assumptions about time. Language is discrete and fairly slow. Physical control is continuous, high-frequency, and very sensitive to small errors. Trying to force one into the shape of the other creates a lot of friction, and you end up spending most of your effort patching mismatches instead of making real progress.

Of course, the honest difficulty is data. The internet gives you trillions of tokens of text, but there's no equivalent ocean of embodied interaction data. That's the main reason people take the shortcut. But I'd rather confront that problem directly, through better ways of collecting real-world data, using video, using simulation and world models, than build on a foundation that I believe has a ceiling.

So it wasn't really stubbornness. It was a bet that if we want machines that truly understand the physical world, they have to grow up in it, so to speak, rather than read about it first and try to catch up later.

r001.rationale: The candidate says adapting models trained on language and internet images is “backwards,” creates friction, and rests on a foundation with a ceiling. This conveys that continuing along that route was not viable as the reason for choosing an embodied-native foundation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came down to a bet about where the bottleneck really is. When I looked at the field, almost everyone was taking a vision-language model that was trained on internet data and then bolting an action head onto it. That's a very natural first step, and it works surprisingly well for demos. But I kept running into the same wall: the model understands the world the way a person describes it in text, not the way a body experiences it. It knows what a cup is, it can even tell you how to pick it up, but it has no real sense of contact, of weight, of timing, of what happens in the two hundred milliseconds after your fingers close.

So the question I asked myself was, is embodiment just a downstream adapter, or is it a different kind of data distribution that should shape the model from the beginning? I became convinced it's the latter. Language is a compressed, lossy description of the physical world. If you only learn from that, you inherit all the gaps that humans never bothered to write down, because they're too obvious to mention. Nobody writes an article about how much force to use when wiping a table. But a robot has to know that.

The second reason is more practical. When you fine-tune a pretrained VLM for actions, you're constantly fighting it. The representation was optimized for answering questions and captioning images, so the action information gets squeezed into whatever space is left over. You can see it in the failure modes: the model is fluent, confident, and physically wrong. I'd rather have a model where perception, action, and even language all share one representation that was built with physical interaction as a first-class citizen from day one.

And I'll be honest, there was a lot of pushback. People said we were throwing away the free lunch of internet-scale pretraining, that we'd never get enough robot data to compete. I don't think it's either-or. We still use web data, we use video, we use simulation. The difference is in what we treat as the center of gravity. For us, the core objective is to predict and control what happens in the physical world, and everything else, including language, is in service of that.

It was a slower road, no question. But I think if you're going to spend years of your life on something, you should bet on what you believe the final form looks like, not on what's easiest to show in the next six months.

r001.rationale: He describes the internet-trained VLM plus action-head approach as hitting a wall and producing physically wrong results, then says embodiment must shape the model from the beginning. This communicates that continuing on the digital-world route was not viable for his goal.

astra-6.text:
Because I think embodiment changes what a model needs to learn. It’s not enough to understand a scene and describe what should happen. The model has to act, observe what changed, and adjust its next action. That interaction with the physical world needs to be part of how it learns from the beginning.

For example, recognizing a cup is different from picking it up. You need to understand where to grasp it, how much force to use, and whether it’s slipping. And your actions affect what you see next. Perception and action are tightly connected.

So by embodied-native, I mean building the model around that connection, rather than treating action as something we attach at the end. Language is still valuable—it helps communicate goals and transfer knowledge—but the model also needs to learn from the consequences of its actions. That’s why I felt this was the right foundation.

r001.rationale: The response says embodiment requires learning through physical action and its consequences, but it does not state that Yujun Shen judged continuing along the digital-world route was not viable.

sol-6.1.text:
Because I think embodiment changes what a model has to learn. If you want a robot to work in the physical world, it’s not enough for it to describe what it sees or explain what should happen next. It has to act, observe the consequences, and adjust.

That’s what I mean by embodied-native: perception, decision-making, and action should be learned together. Imagine picking up a cup. Recognizing the cup is only one part of the task. You also need to understand where to grasp it, how much force to apply, and what to do if it slips. Your own action changes the next observation.

So the reason for insisting on this approach is that I see that interaction loop as fundamental. I want the model to learn how its actions affect the world, and to use that understanding to handle situations it hasn’t encountered before.

r001.rationale: The response says embodiment and real-world interaction are fundamental, but does not state that continuing along the digital-world route was not viable.
